papers_read.title_as_printed: Tortuosity and discrete compactness biomarkers for machine learning-based classification of mild cognitive impairment (Torres Guzman et al., Biomed Signal Process Control 2026)

Automated classification of Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, and cognitively normal patients using 3D convolutional neural network and radiomic features from T1-weighted brain MRI: A comparative study on detection accuracy (Zarei et al., Clinical Imaging 2024)

what_each_reports.P-125: MCI vs HC, ADNI 1.5T, 74 subjects (37/37), 8 amygdala morphometric features (volume, normalised volume, discrete compactness, tortuosity). Abstract: test accuracy 82.14%. Results/Table 6: mean test accuracy 80.00 +/-2.43 (RF), 79.29 (SVM), 77.86 (KNN), 80.00 (ANN); test AUC 85.71-90.31%. 60/40 subject split, about 30 test subjects.
what_each_reports.P-66: MCI vs CN, ADNI, 200 MCI + 200 CN (948 + 853 images), hippocampus + amygdala ROIs, 1746 radiomic features per ROI fused with a 3D CNN, plus age/sex: ACC 72.7 +/-3.3%, AUC 80 (Table 6). Radiomics alone 71.6%; CNN alone 69.0%; amygdala-only fusion 70.0%. The train/test split is at image level (80/20 of images).

quantity_a: Test accuracy for MCI vs HC in ADNI from 8 hand-crafted amygdala shape/volume features (RF/SVM/KNN/ANN), n=74, subject-level hold-out
quantity_b: Test accuracy for MCI vs CN in ADNI from hippocampus+amygdala radiomics (4 x 1746 features) fused with 3D-CNN features and age/sex, n=400 subjects / 1801 images, image-level split
incompatible_if_same: No. These are two different predictor sets each reporting a different score, and neither paper claims an ordering the other refutes. P-125's test set is about 28-30 subjects, so the binomial standard error of its accuracy is about 7-8 points, and 72.7% lies within that uncertainty of 80%.

gates.task: match: both MCI vs CN/HC (T1). P-66's registry row is coded T3, but the binary MCI-vs-CN result exists.
gates.validation_tier: match nominally (both internal, V2). Split units differ: P-125 splits by subject; P-66 splits images, with multiple images per subject.

endpoint_and_metric: compatible metric (accuracy, same comparison). The predictor set and input representation differ: 8 amygdala morphometric scalars vs thousands of hippocampal+amygdala radiomic features plus CNN features plus demographics.
performance_validity: flag does not apply: no result at or above 0.97 (P-125 best test AUC 90.31%; P-66 AUC 80)
independence: Both use ADNI, so subject overlap is possible. No shared authors (Mexico vs Iran/USA groups).
grounds: The two accuracies come from different predictor sets and input representations (8 amygdala shape/volume features vs radiomics+CNN on two ROIs). This is the same substrate difference that led C-80 to be reclassified as documented incommensurability.
P-66 splits its data by images rather than subjects, so its test accuracy is not the same estimand as P-125's subject-level hold-out.
Even read as one quantity, the two values are not incompatible given P-125's roughly 30-subject test set, and neither paper claims the ordering the other would refute.

record_defects: claim_a 82.14% is the abstract figure only. P-125's Results and Table 6 give a best mean test accuracy of 80.00%, and 82.14% does not appear in its results tables.
resolution_note 'Metric type unclear: Acc / Unknown' is wrong: both values are accuracy.
P-66's registry row (T3, Best_Metric AUC 0.80) differs from the record's binary claim. The record's 72.7% MCI-vs-CN value is correct against the PDF.
what_would_change_the_verdict: The same feature set and the same subject-level protocol applied in both studies, with non-overlapping uncertainty. Neither document provides this.
